01.note: Onkelos bar Kelonimos, a Roman, converted to Judaism, and the emperor sent a troop of soldiers to seize him. Onkelos drew them in with verses, and they converted. A second troop, told not to say anything to him, heard him point out that every official holds a torch before a greater one, yet God held a torch before the Jewish people in the wilderness; they converted too. A third troop, told not to converse with him at all, saw him put his hand on a mezuza and explain that God guards His servants from outside their homes. They also converted, and after that the emperor sent no more soldiers after him.
01.why: The Gemara has been telling of Romans drawn to Judaism, such as Ketia and Antoninus, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's companion; this account of Onkelos continues that thread before the discussion returns to Antoninus.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kelonimos
people.about: A Roman who converted to Judaism and won over the soldiers sent to arrest him.

people.name: The emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who sent three troops of soldiers to bring Onkelos back.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with verses from the Torah, fixed to the doorpost of a Jewish home.

terms.term: the Holy One, Blessed be He
terms.meaning: A common rabbinic way of referring to God.

02.note: Shmuel describes a festival held in Rome once every seventy years. A healthy man is made to ride on a lame man, dressed in the garments of Adam, the first man, with the scalp of the executed sage Rabbi Yishmael on his head and gold hung on his neck, while the markets are covered with onyx. Heralds announce before him that Jacob's calculation of the redemption is fraudulent and that Esau is a forger, and they end: Woe to this one, Esau, when that one, Jacob, will arise.
02.why: The mishna lists the festivals of the gentiles, and the Gemara adds this Roman one; right after, it explains that the mishna leaves it out because it lists only festivals held every year.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who describes the festival, as reported by his student Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage whose scalp, flayed by the Romans when they executed him, is placed on the rider's head.

terms.meaning: The twin sons of Isaac and Rebecca. The Sages read Esau as a symbol of Rome and Jacob as a symbol of the Jewish people; Jacob limped after wrestling with an angel.

02.flag: This describes a recurring Roman ritual rather than a single event.

03.note: Rabbi Yosei recalls an incident: Yosef the priest followed his teacher to the city of Sidon, outside the Land of Israel, in order to learn Torah. Rabbi Yohanan rules that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
03.why: A baraita asks whether a priest may leave the Land of Israel, and so become ritually impure, to study Torah when teachers are available at home. Rabbi Yosei says he may, since one does not learn from everyone, and cites Yosef the priest as precedent.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells of the incident to support his ruling.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest who left the Land of Israel to follow his teacher to Sidon to learn Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who rules that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron (a kohen). Priests must avoid certain kinds of ritual impurity, and the Sages treated lands outside Israel as impure.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

04.note: Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household had to present the authorities with a fattened ox on their festival day. They paid forty thousand dinars so they could bring it the day after the festival instead, another forty thousand so they could bring it slaughtered rather than alive, and another forty thousand so they would not have to bring it at all.
04.why: The Gemara asks whether one may sell a gentile a fattened ox, which might later be kept for work, and tries this case as proof. It rejects the proof: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi simply wanted to end the practice step by step.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The head of the household that paid to escape the gift of an ox; called simply Rabbi in the text.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident, through Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; forty thousand dinars was a very large sum.
An ox fed up for slaughter rather than kept for plowing or other work.

05.note: Rabbi Eliezer was arrested on a charge of heresy and brought before a tribunal. When the officer asked why an elder like him would engage in such frivolous matters, he answered that he trusted the Judge, meaning God; the officer thought he meant him and acquitted him. At home Rabbi Eliezer refused his students' consolation, until Rabbi Akiva suggested he had once enjoyed some heretical teaching. Rabbi Eliezer remembered meeting Ya'akov of Kefar Sekhanya, a student of Jesus the Nazarene, in the market of Tzippori, who taught him an interpretation of a verse in Jesus' name that pleased him. He concluded that this was why he had been arrested, since he had come too close to heresy.
05.why: The mishna forbids helping gentiles build a tribunal, a place where people are sentenced to death; this leads the Gemara to tell of Sages who were brought before the Roman authorities for judgment.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage arrested for heresy and acquitted, who later traced his arrest to a heretic's teaching he had enjoyed.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who helps him see why he was arrested.

people.name: Ya'akov of Kefar Sekhanya
people.about: A student of Jesus the Nazarene whom Rabbi Eliezer met in the market of Tzippori.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: The teacher in whose name Ya'akov passed on the interpretation.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who rules that one must keep four cubits from a prostitute.

terms.meaning: Here, the teachings of sectarian groups the Sages considered outside Judaism, including early followers of Jesus.
The Torah forbids bringing a prostitute's fee as an offering to the Temple; Ya'akov asked whether it could pay for a bathroom for the High Priest.
An ancient measure of length, roughly half a meter; four cubits is about two meters.

06.note: A woman came to Rav Hisda to confess her sins and said that the lightest of them was that she had conceived her younger son by her older son. Rav Hisda told her to prepare her funeral shrouds. In one version she did not die; in another version she died.
06.why: The Gemara has just read a verse to mean that those who leave heresy do not live long. It uses this woman, who from her words must also have been a heretic, to test that idea, answering that in the first version she had not truly repented.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage before whom the woman confessed, who told her to prepare her shrouds.

terms.meaning: Here, belonging to a sect the Sages considered outside Judaism. The Gemara infers that if incest was her lightest sin, she was also a heretic.

07.note: Elazar ben Durdayya had been with every prostitute in the world. Hearing of one overseas who charged a purse of dinars, he took the money and crossed seven rivers to reach her; during the act she passed wind and said that, like the wind, he would never be accepted in repentance. Shaken, he sat between mountains and begged the mountains and hills, heaven and earth, sun and moon, and stars and constellations to pray for mercy for him, and each said it must pray for itself. Concluding that it depended only on him, he put his head between his knees and cried until his soul left him. A Divine Voice declared him destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept that some acquire their world in one moment, adding that penitents are even called Rabbi.
07.why: The Gemara has claimed that a heretic who repents dies soon after, and asks whether that is true of sexual sin too. Elazar ben Durdayya died on repenting; the Gemara answers that his attachment to sin was so strong it resembled heresy.

people.name: Elazar ben Durdayya
people.about: A man notorious for visiting prostitutes, who repented and died weeping.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he wept on hearing the story and said penitents are even called Rabbi.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's decision, a common device in rabbinic stories.
The life of reward after this world.

08.note: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were walking and came to a fork: one path led past a place of idol worship, the other past a brothel. One proposed the idol path, since the urge for idol worship had been slaughtered; the other proposed the brothel path, so they could overcome their urge and be rewarded. When they got there, the prostitutes withdrew before them. Asked how he had known this would happen, the second cited the verse that discernment will guard you from lewdness.
08.why: The Gemara has been teaching that one must keep far from heresy and from prostitutes; this story of two Sages choosing their path between idol worship and a brothel follows on that theme.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage walking with Rabbi Yonatan; the text does not say which of the two proposed which path.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: A Sage walking with Rabbi Hanina.

terms.meaning: The inner urge to sin. The Sages taught that the urge to worship idols had been slaughtered, that is, removed from the world.

09.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata and Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon were arrested by the Romans. Elazar envied Hanina for facing one charge against his own five, but Hanina said Elazar would be saved because he had practiced acts of kindness as well as Torah, while he himself had only studied. At his trial Elazar denied teaching Torah and stealing, called himself master of weavers, and was saved by miracles: hornets showed him the warp and the woof, an old man was trampled the day he claimed to fear trampling, and Elijah threw away the man who would have testified against him. Hanina answered that he studied Torah as God commanded him, and he was sentenced to burning, his wife to execution and his daughter to a brothel.
09.why: The Gemara is telling of Sages tried by the Roman authorities, which grew out of the mishna's ban on building a tribunal with gentiles. Along the way it explains Hanina's sentence: he pronounced God's name in public, and his wife did not protest.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata
people.about: A Sage arrested on five charges, who was saved by a series of miracles.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage arrested for teaching Torah and sentenced to death by burning.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as a Roman nobleman and removes the witness against Rabbi Elazar.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who teaches that one who studies Torah alone is like one who has no God.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov
people.about: A Sage who said charity should be given only when someone like Hanina ben Teradyon oversees it.

terms.meaning: The two sets of threads in weaving: the warp is fixed on the loom, and the woof is passed through it.
God's four-letter name, which may not be pronounced as it is written.
A meeting place where debates on wisdom and faith were held.
A Persian unit of distance, a few kilometers; four hundred parasangs is a vast distance.

09.flag: The story stops before the reason for the daughter's sentence and the family's acceptance of the verdict, which follow directly after.

10.note: Rabbi Yohanan tells that the daughter of Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon was once walking before the nobles of Rome, who remarked on how pleasant her steps were. At once she took care to keep walking so that her steps would go on pleasing them. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish links this to the verse "The iniquity of my heel encircles me": the small sins a person tramples underfoot in this world surround him on the Day of Judgment.
10.why: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's daughter was sentenced to sit in a brothel; the Gemara, having explained why he and his wife were punished, asks why she was, and this incident is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: Her father, a Sage condemned by the Romans.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: A Sage whose reading of a verse in Psalms the Gemara links to the incident.

terms.meaning: The time when God judges each person's deeds.

11.note: As Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon, his wife and his daughter went out after being sentenced, each of them accepted God's judgment as just with a verse. He said, "The Rock, His work is perfect"; his wife continued, "A God of faithfulness and without iniquity"; and his daughter said, "Great in counsel, and mighty in work." Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: How great these righteous people are, that three verses of accepting judgment came to them at the moment they accepted it.
11.why: The Gemara has just explained why Heaven decreed each of the three sentences, his for saying God's name in public, his wife's for not protesting, his daughter's for her vanity; now it shows all three accepting the verdict as just.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage sentenced by the Romans to death by burning.

people.name: His wife
people.about: Sentenced to execution; she completes her husband's verse.

people.name: His daughter
people.about: Sentenced to sit in a brothel; she adds a verse from Jeremiah.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he praises the three for their verses.

terms.meaning: Declaring that God's decree is just even when it brings suffering; still part of Jewish mourning practice.

12.note: When Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma fell ill, Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon visited him and was warned that Rome would burn him and his Torah scroll for teaching in public. Asked if he had a place in the World-to-Come, Hanina told how he gave his own Purim money to the poor, and Yosei wished to share his lot. Days later Yosei died, and Roman notables returning from his funeral found Hanina teaching in public. They wrapped him in his scroll and burned him, with wet wool on his heart to slow his death. He saw the letters flying upward and would not open his mouth to the fire. The executioner raised the flame and removed the wool for a promise of the World-to-Come, then leaped into the fire; a Divine Voice declared both destined for it, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept.
12.why: The Gemara has been following Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's arrest and sentence by the Romans, and here tells how the sentence of burning was carried out.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma
people.about: A Sage, called teacher by Hanina, who warned him that Rome would burn him.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage who kept teaching Torah in public and was burned alive by the Romans.

people.name: His daughter
people.about: Watches her father's burning and asks how she can see him like this.

people.name: The executioner
people.about: The Roman who hastened Hanina's death and then threw himself into the fire.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he wept on hearing what the Divine Voice declared.

terms.meaning: Money set aside for the festival of Purim. Hanina mixed his up with charity funds and gave all of it to the poor.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's decision.
The life of reward after this world.

13.note: Berurya, Rabbi Meir's wife, could not bear that her sister was sitting in a brothel, so Rabbi Meir took a vessel of dinars and went, reasoning that a miracle would happen only if she had not sinned. Disguised as a knight, he propositioned her; she put him off, and he concluded she had done no wrong. He gave her guard the money and taught him to say "God of Meir answer me!", proving it by escaping man-eating dogs, and the guard handed her over. Later the guard was taken to be hanged, said the words and was let down, and told the whole story; the Romans engraved Rabbi Meir's face at the gate of Rome. Chased one day, he ducked into a brothel and escaped, either by pretending to eat gentile food or because Elijah, disguised as a prostitute, embraced him; then he fled to Babylonia.
13.why: The Gemara has just told that the Romans sentenced Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's daughter to sit in a brothel, and explained why Heaven allowed it; this tells how her sister's husband rescued her.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Rabbi Meir's wife, a daughter of Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon, who asks him to save her sister.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who rescues his wife's sister from a Roman brothel and becomes a hunted man.

people.name: The guard
people.about: The man guarding the sister, who takes the bribe and is later saved from hanging.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who in one version appears as a prostitute to save Rabbi Meir from capture.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; a vessel full of them was a large fortune.
The Sages forbade Jews to eat it, so the Romans would not believe that a man eating it could be Rabbi Meir.

14.note: Levi and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, were studying before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. When they finished a book, Levi asked for Proverbs and Rabbi Shimon for Psalms; Rabbi Shimon overruled Levi, and Psalms was brought. When they reached the verse "But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord", Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explained that a person can learn Torah only from the part his heart desires. Levi said: My teacher, you have just given me permission to get up and leave.
14.why: The Gemara has quoted Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's teaching that one learns only what his heart desires; this incident shows the occasion on which he said it, and how his student turned it back on him.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi who wanted to study Proverbs.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who insisted on studying Psalms.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; the teacher of both, and Rabbi Shimon's father.

15.note: Rav Hisda told the Sages studying with him that he wanted to tell them something but was afraid that they would then leave him: that anyone who learns Torah from one teacher never sees a sign of blessing. They did leave him and went to learn from Rava. Rav Hisda then told them that this applies only to reasoning; for learning the tradition itself it is better to have one teacher, so as not to be confused by different versions.
15.why: The school of Rabbi Yannai has just read the verse comparing a scholar to a replanted tree to mean that one should learn from many teachers; Rav Hisda's students act on exactly that teaching, and he limits it.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who feared his students would leave him, and did lose them to Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage to whom Rav Hisda's students went.

people.name: Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai
people.about: A Sage who teaches that one should divide one's study into Bible, Mishna and Talmud.

terms.meaning: The memorized oral teachings themselves, as opposed to the reasoning used to analyze them.

15.flag: The last segment adds Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai's separate teaching on dividing one's study, which is not part of the Rav Hisda incident.

16.note: Rabbi Alexandri would call out in public like a merchant selling his wares: Who wants life? Who wants life? Everyone crowded around him, saying: Give us life! He answered them with the verse "Who is the man that desires life... Keep your tongue from evil."
16.why: The Gemara is collecting teachings that Torah study brings success; right after this verse it explains that the psalm's next words, "do good", mean studying Torah, not only avoiding evil speech.

people.name: Rabbi Alexandri
people.about: A Sage who called out in the street offering life to anyone who wanted it.

17.note: Two incidents are told. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount, saw an exceptionally beautiful gentile woman and said, "How great are Your works, O Lord!" Rabbi Akiva saw the wife of the wicked Turnus Rufus and spat, laughed and cried: he spat because she came from a putrid drop, laughed because she was destined to convert and he would marry her, and cried because such beauty would end up consumed by dirt.
17.why: Rav has ruled that one may not say how beautiful a gentile woman is. The Gemara raises these incidents as an objection, and answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was thanking God for His creatures, not praising the woman.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage who praised God on seeing a beautiful gentile woman.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who spat, laughed and cried on seeing the wife of Turnus Rufus.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: Called wicked in the text; his wife was destined to convert and marry Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: The hill in Jerusalem on which the Temple stood.
A blunt rabbinic phrase for the seed from which every person is conceived, a reminder of human lowliness.

18.note: This is a short answer, not a full story. The Gemara explains that Rabban Gamliel did not look at the beautiful woman on purpose: he was walking around a corner, and they came upon each other unexpectedly as each of them turned.
18.why: A baraita has just taught that a man may not gaze at a beautiful woman; this answers how the Sage in the earlier incident, who saw a beautiful gentile woman on the Temple Mount and praised God, could have looked at her.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who saw the beautiful woman; the translation explains he met her by chance at a corner.

18.flag: The STORY is a single three-word answer ("it was a corner") to a question about an incident told earlier; it has no events of its own.

19.note: Some saffron growers, a gentile and a Jew, shared a field: the gentile worked it on Shabbat and the Jew on Sunday. They came before Rava, who permitted the arrangement. Ravina challenged him with a baraita that allows such a split only if it was agreed at the outset, and Rava was embarrassed; in the end it came out that the partners had agreed on it from the start.
19.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a Jew may let a gentile or Samaritan work his field on days when Jews may not work. Right after, it gives another version of the case, and then says Ravina meant to support Rava and the embarrassment never happened.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who permitted the partnership.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava's ruling from a baraita.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which Jews may not work and may not profit from work done for them.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.

20.note: Two Sages report what they saw. Rabbi Hanina, as Shmuel quotes him, saw a gentile buy a goose in the market, have sex with it, strangle it, roast it and eat it. Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti saw an Arab buy a thigh of meat in the market, carve a hole in it for penetration, penetrate it, roast it and eat it.
20.why: The discussion has been about why a Jew may not leave his animals alone with gentiles, whom it suspects of bestiality. It now asks whether the same holds for birds, and these reports are its proof that it does.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who reports seeing a gentile abuse a goose; quoted by Shmuel through Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
people.about: A Sage who reports what he saw an Arab do with a thigh of meat.

terms.meaning: Sexual relations with an animal, which the Torah forbids.
